topic: Access Specifiers and Name Visibility in Namespaces and Classes
explanation: In C++, access specifiers (public, private, protected) control the visibility and accessibility of class members and nested types. When referring to nested types or members via qualified names (e.g., A::B), the accessibility depends on their declared access level. Public nested types are accessible outside the class or namespace, while private or protected nested types are inaccessible from outside, leading to compile-time errors. Understanding how access specifiers influence name visibility is essential for designing encapsulated, modular, and correct C++ code.
code_example: A::BB x; // OK, BB is public, accessible outside namespace
A::B y; // Error, B is private, inaccessible outside namespace
example_explanation: This example demonstrates how access specifiers affect the visibility of nested types within a namespace. 'A::BB' is declared as public, so it can be instantiated outside the namespace. Conversely, 'A::B' is private, so attempting to instantiate it outside the namespace results in a compile-time error. This illustrates the importance of access control in managing name visibility and encapsulation in C++.
